title: Combining Student Scores: Why Adding Subjects Is Trickier Than It Looks
author: Dylan Wiliam
summary: Wiliam presents a decisive example exposing why aggregating scores across subjects is not straightforward: when one subject has a 90-point spread (10 to 100) and another a 20-point spread (40 to 60), raw totals are dominated by the wide-spread subject. Converting to class ranks throws away real information about gap size. A better approach rescales each subject from 0 to 100 with lowest and highest scores at extremes and everyone else proportionally in between. When Wiliam applies this rescaling, the student who topped the raw table ends up at the bottom and vice versa. The point is not that any one method is correct, but that the choice of method is a choice about what we think overall performance means, and that choice is rarely made explicit. School leaders generating league tables, teachers computing overall grades, and parents reading composite reports all operate on assumptions that are usually wrong in ways that meaningfully reorder who looks strong.
points: Aggregating scores across subjects is not as straightforward as adding raw percentages; subjects with wider spreads dominate totals regardless of meaningful learning differences.
The choice of scaling method (raw totals, class ranks, or rescaling to 0-100) is a choice about what 'overall performance' means, and that choice is rarely made explicit.
Different scaling methods can meaningfully reorder who looks strong and who looks weak; composite scores require transparency about which assumptions are being made.
quotes: One example that Paul shared with me really got me thinking about what happens when we add scores from different subjects.

If we have a group of 12 students, and have their percentage scores on 8 subjects, it might seem easy to work out who is the best students. We just add up the scores on each of the 8 subjects, and see who has the highest total.
However, there is a problem here. Subject 1 used most of the mark range, with scores ranging from 10 to 100, while others, such as subject 3, have scores ranging only from 40 to 60.
To control for this, we could replace scores with class ranks, giving the highest scoring student in each subject a rank of 1, and the lowest scoring student a rank of 12.
However, when we use ranks, we throw away information, because we take no account of how much better the first ranked student is than the lowest ranked student; the difference will always be 11.

Instead, a better approach might be to scale the scores so that every subject uses the full range of scores from 0 to 100, with the lowest scoring student getting 0, the highest scoring student getting 100, and the others scaled in between.
Now, the student who was top — Adams — is at the bottom, and the student who was at the bottom — Lant — is at the top.
If that doesn’t make you realize that adding up scores like this is not as straightforward as it seems, I don’t know what will.” Archived from Dylan Wiliam on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
